column2: Then in the future creation, in the Krita age again, they will serve as the seed of the brahmin and kshatriya orders once more.
In the same way, in all the ages the Seven Sages remain here together with the kings for the sake of continuing the lineages.
The connection of the kshatriyas with their extinction is remembered by the twice-born; the lineage of the seven Manu periods has been heard by you.
The origin of brahmins and kshatriyas proceeds from age to age; as their beginning is, so is the decline of those who have come forth.
The Seven Sages, being long-lived, know their rise and fall. In this sequence the twice-born of the Aila and Ikshvaku lines,
arising in the Treta age and declining again in Kali, follow the course of the ages until the Manu period ends.
When the kshatriyas had been wholly destroyed by Rama son of Jamadagni, this whole earth was again filled with kshatriya rulers.
I shall also tell the cause of the two lineages; listen. The nature of the Aila and Ikshvaku lines changes over time.
The kings are arranged in succession, and likewise other kshatriya rulers — those famed in the Aila line and the Ikshvaku kings.
A full hundred and one of their families were consecrated; the expansion of the Bhojas is remembered as twice as many.
The kshatriya order occupies three portions, and the fourth by its direction. Hear from me those among them who are past.
A hundred Prativindhyas, a hundred Nagas with the Haihayas, a hundred and one Dhritarashtras and eighty Janamejayas,
a hundred Brahmadattas, a hundred Sharins and Virins, then a hundred Paulas, the Shvetakashyas, Kushas and others,
and a further thousand Shashabindus who are past; all of them performed horse sacrifices with gifts of a million.
Thus royal sages have passed by hundreds and thousands. Of those in this present interval of Vaivasvata Manu,
hear of the lineages remembered as arising in the world. The full detail of those lineages in relation to one another cannot be told,
even in hundreds of years, following earlier and later connections. Twenty-eight ages have passed in the Vaivasvata interval.
Hear of those that remain, along with these royal sages: forty-three are yet to come with their kings.
When those ages remain no more, the Vaivasvata period will end. All this has been told to you in brief and in detail.
Because of much repetition it cannot be told along with the ages. These are the five lineages of Yayati's sons, for the good of the people.
They have been recounted — the past ones who uphold the worlds. One who hears them obtains five boons rare in this world:
long life, fame, wealth, sons and heaven, and attains endlessness — by remembering and hearing of the five lineages of the wise one.
Thus, O twice-born, I have told you this third quarter in detail and in order. What more shall I describe?
Sukarmans, Sutaras, the learned Sahasrada, Parvata, Anuchara, Apashu and Manojava,
Urja, Svaha, Svadha and Tara — these ten are remembered as the Haritas. Tapas, Jnani, Mriti, Varcha and the one remembered as Bandhu,
Rajas, Raja, Svarnapada, Pushti and Vidhi — these ten gods are remembered as the Rohitas.
The gods beginning with the Tushitas are declared to be thirty-three. Know them as the Sumanas; now hear of the Sukarmans.
Suparvan, Vrishabha, Prishta, Kapi, Dyumna, Vipashchit, Vikrama, Krama, Vibhrita and Kanta —
these gods are the Sukarmans; now hear of the Sutaras: Varsha, Divya, Anjishtha, Varchasvin, Dyutiman, Kavi,
Shubha, Havis, Kritaprapti and Vyaprita the tenth — these gods are declared by name as the Sutaras.
Their Indra should be known as the glorious Ritadhaman. Dyuti son of Vasishtha, Sutapas of Atri's line,
Tapomurti of Angiras's line, Tapasvin of Kashyapa's, Taponidhi of Pulastya's and Taporati of Pulaha's,
and the seventh, of Bhrigu's line, should be known as Tapodhriti. These are the perfected Seven Sages in the last Savarnika interval.
Devavan, Upadeva, Devashreshtha, Viduratha, Mitravan, Mitrasena, Chitrasena, Amitraha,
Mitrabahu and Suvarchas are the sons of the twelfth Manu. In the thirteenth turn, in the future Rauchya interval,
three groups of gods have been declared by the Self-born; they are all great-souled mind-born sons of Brahma:
the Sutramans, the Sudharmans and the Sukarmans — these three are declared the future groups of the thirty gods who drink Soma.
The thirty-three deities who are worshipped separately by sacrificers with ghee, with curdled ghee and with the best of cups —
know those thirty-three gods separately. The Sutramans are the Prayaja deities who now partake of ghee;
the Sukarmans are the Anuyaja deities who partake of curdled ghee; the Sudharmans are the Upayajas — so these gods are declared.
Their Indra will be Divaspati of great strength. The sons of Ruchi should be known as sons of Pulaha's offspring.
Dhritiman of Angiras's line, Avyaya of Pulastya's line, Tattvadarshin of Pulaha's line, Nirutsuka of Bhrigu's line,
Nishprakampya of Atri's line, Nirmoha of Kashyapa's and Sutapas of Vasishtha's — these seven belong to the thirteenth interval.
Chitrasena, Vichitra, Naya, Dharma, Dhrita, Bhava, Aneka, Kshatraviddha, Surasa and Nirbhaya — these ten
are the sons of Rauchya Manu in the thirteenth interval. In the fourteenth turn, the interval of Bhautya Manu,
five groups of gods are declared who will be: the Chakshushas, Pavitras, Kanishthas, Bhrajitas
and Vachavriddhas — these are remembered as the five groups of gods. Know the seven musical notes beginning with Nishada as the seven Chakshushas;
the Samans beginning with Brihat are known as the seven Kanishthas; the seven worlds are the Pavitras, and the seven rivers the Bhrajitas;
know the Vachavriddhas as the sages of Svayambhuva Manu. All the Indras of the Manu periods should be known as having similar characteristics.
By splendour, austerity, intellect, strength, learning and valour — whatever beings there are in the three worlds, moving and fixed,
those Indras surpass them all in every respect and in all qualities. There are the joyous ones who deny beings, the neutral ones who affirm beings,
and those who affirm both existence and non-existence; the three Vedas are the authority of those who speak. Agnidhra of Kashyapa's line, the one of Pulastya's line who is Magadha,
Agnibahu of Bhrigu's line, Shuchi of Angiras's line, Shukra of Vasishtha's line, Mukta of Pulaha's line,
and Shvajita of Atri's line are declared; now hear of the sons of Manu: Uru, Guru, Gambhira, Buddha, Shuddha, Shuchi, Kritin,
Urjasvin and Subala — these are the sons of Bhautya Manu. These four Savarna Manus are sons of Brahma;
one, Vaivasvata, is also called Savarna Manu. Rauchya and Bhautya are considered to be of the lines of Pulaha and Bhrigu. During the reign of Bhautya the kalpa is swiftly completed.
Suta said: When all the Manu periods here have been completed,
at the end, when that many-aged period has waned, the dissolution is declared. These seven Bhargava gods, at the end of the Manu period,
having enjoyed the three worlds from their place for seventy-one ages, together with the ancestors and the Manus, when the Manu period has ended —
then this whole three-world universe will be without support. Then the shining abodes of those who dwell in them,
released, fall away, along with the stars, constellations and planets. Then, when those lords of the three worlds have passed away,
they reach the Mahar world where the dwellers of the kalpa live — where the fourteen long-lived groups beginning with the Ajitas are.
Those fourteen gods of all the Manu periods are said to dwell in the Jana world in their bodies, together with their followers.
When the gods have thus passed from the Mahar world to the Jana world, and only the fixed beings remain among the elements,
when the world-regions beginning with Bhuvar are empty and the gods have gone upward to union with the dwellers of the kalpa,
then Brahma, having withdrawn the gods, sages, ancestors and Danavas, sets aside creation, seeing the day end at the close of the ages.
Those who know day and night know that a day of Brahma ends after a thousand four-age cycles, and his night likewise ends after a thousand ages.
The occasional, the elemental and the absolute — thus is the threefold dissolution of all beings.
Brahma's occasional dissolution is the burning at the end of the kalpa; the elemental is the dissolution of the instruments at the re-creation of beings;
and the absolute, arising from knowledge, is declared to be the non-arising of the causes. Then Brahma, having withdrawn the gods who dwell in the three worlds,
strikes and brings about the dissolution of creation again. Wishing to sleep, the Lord Brahma then withdraws the creatures.
Then, at the end of a thousand ages, when the destruction of the ages arrives, that Prajapati resolves to hold the creatures within himself.
Then there is an unbroken drought lasting a hundred years. Through it, the beings of little strength on the surface of the earth
perish right there and turn into earth. The fire, becoming the sun with seven rays, rose up.
The Lord of unbearable rays drinks up the waters with his beams; his seventy blazing rays, tawny in hue,
spread out again and slowly pervade the sky. Earthly fire fed on wood blazes fiercely, and the sun blazes with the waters.
Therefore the sun is said to burn by holding water. The sun does not blaze without rain, nor is it moistened without rain;
without rain it would not enter; the sun blazes with water. Therefore the sun, drinking the waters, blazes in the sky.
His seven rays drink water from the great ocean; kindled by that food, they become seven suns.
Then those seven rays, become suns in the four directions, blaze as fires and burn this entire fourfold world.
With those rays they reach above and below; the seven suns blaze with the heat of the fire at the end of the age.
Kindled by the water, with many thousands of rays, they stand covering the whole, burning up the earth.
Then, burned by their heat, the earth with its mountains, rivers and oceans becomes utterly dry.
With blazing, continuous and brilliant rays of the sun it is hemmed in on all sides, below, above and across.
The fires of the suns, growing and mingling with one another, becoming one, form a single flame.
That fire, destroyer of all worlds, becoming a circle, swiftly burns this entire fourfold world with its heat.
Then, when everything moving and unmoving has perished, the earth, bare of trees and grass, becomes like the back of a tortoise.
The whole world appears like a frying pan; filled everywhere with those flames, it blazes densely.
The beings on the earth's surface and those in the great ocean then perish and turn into earth.
Continents, mountains, regions and the great ocean — that all-consuming fire reduced them all to ashes.
The kindled fire, blazing and resting on the earth, drinks the waters from the oceans, rivers and netherworlds everywhere.
Then, growing greater, overpassing the mountains and the planets, the blazing, terrible Samvartaka fire destroys the worlds.
Then, piercing the earth, it dried up Rasatala; having burned the netherworlds at the end, it burned the world of wind.
Having burned the earth below, it burned heaven above; for thousands, millions and hundreds of millions of yojanas
the many flames of that Samvartaka rose up. The Gandharvas, Pishachas, great serpents and Rakshasas,
and the whole sphere, it then burns, blazing: the Bhur world, the Bhuvar world, the Svar world and Mahar as well.
Thus the terrible fire of time burns the four worlds. When those worlds are pervaded by fire across and above,
this whole world, slowly reached by that heat, then appears like a ball of iron.
Then, shaped like herds of elephants and adorned with lightning, the terrible Samvartaka clouds rise in the sky.
Some are dark as blue lotuses, some like white water-lilies, some like beryl, others like sapphire,
others like conch and jasmine, or like fine collyrium; some clouds are smoke-coloured, some rain-clouds yellow,
some the colour of donkeys, some like lac juice, others like red arsenic, and clouds the colour of doves;
some like the cochineal insect, others like yellow orpiment, some like the feathers of the blue jay — such clouds rise in the sky.
Some shaped like fine cities, some like herds of elephants, some like mountains, some clouds like level ground,
some like pleasure-houses, some like shoals of fish — many-formed, terrible in form, roaring with dreadful sounds.
Then all the clouds fill the expanse of the sky. Then those clouds, of terrible roar and born of the sun,
enveloped in seven layers, quench that fire. Then those clouds pour down rain like a great flood,
and destroy the very terrible, inauspicious fire entirely. With the torrential rain the world is filled with water.
The fire, overpowered by the waters, then enters the waters. When the fire is gone, the clouds born of fire, having rained,
flood the whole world with great streams of water, filling it with torrents as they are impelled by the Self-born.
Others with floods of water overrun the shoreline; the water, having covered the mountains and the regions between the continents, remains.
Again it falls on the earth, and the clouds on the vault of the sky; the terrible wind encircles the heavens on every side.
In that terrible single ocean, when all moving and unmoving things have perished, after a full thousand ages the kalpa is said to be complete.
When the world is covered with water, the wise call it the single ocean; then earth, water, sky and wind are one ocean.
When the fire has gone out and all has become dark, nothing whatever can be discerned. The waters of earth, of the ocean and of heaven, everywhere,
no longer flowing, come to oneness and take the name of 'salila'. Because it comes and goes, that water is then called 'salila'.
That water, called the ocean (arnava), covers this earth. Because it shines (abhati) with its lustre — the root 'bha' meaning pervasion and shining —
and reaches all as ash (bhasma), it is therefore called 'ambhas'. In the sense of diversity and swiftness the root 'ar' is used;
but in the single ocean it is not swift, hence the waters are called 'nara'. At the end of that thousand ages, when Brahma's day has passed,
the world remains a single ocean for that same length of time. Then all the activities of Prajapati cease.
In that single ocean, when moving and unmoving things have perished, Brahma then becomes thousand-eyed and thousand-footed —
thousand-headed, benevolent, thousand-footed, thousand-eyed and thousand-mouthed, thousand-voiced, thousand-armed, the first Prajapati, the Person said to consist of the threefold Veda,
sun-coloured, protector of the world, unprecedented, the one, the first, the victorious; Hiranyagarbha, the great Person, is proclaimed as beyond passion.
At the end of a thousand four-age cycles, when all is flooded with water, the Lord, wishing to sleep and to be unmanifest, makes night.
When all four kinds of creatures lie dissolved, the seven great sages behold that great soul, Time; they dwell in the Jana world, having gained vision through austerity —
the great souls beginning with Bhrigu, whose characteristics were described earlier.
With their vision they behold the seven worlds beginning with Satya, and they always behold Brahma during the nights of Brahma.
The Seven Sages behold the time of sleep during his nights. Because he is supreme among the kalpas, he is called the first.
He is the creator of all beings again and again at the beginnings of the kalpas. Having thus lain down within himself, Prajapati,
of great splendour and maker of all, having taken everything into himself, then spends the night in the darkness, in the waters of the single ocean.
Then, when the night ends, Prajapati awakens; his mind joined with the wish to create, he sets himself again to creation.
Thus when the world has ceased and Prajapati is at rest, in that occasional dissolution of Brahma,
the separation of beings from their bodies is remembered as complete. Then, when all beings have been burned by the rays of the sun,
and the best of gods, sages and Manus are in that flood of waters, all beings from the Gandharvas down to the Pishachas,
unburned at the beginning of the kalpa, take refuge in the Jana world. Those that had gone to animal births or to hell
are then also burned, their sins wholly shaken off; they remain in the water as long as the world is flooded.
When the night has dawned, all those beings are born again completely from Brahma, whose source is the unmanifest —
sages, Manus, gods and all four kinds of creatures. Even for the perfected ones, death and birth are declared.
As the rising and setting of the sun are known in this world, so the birth and cessation of beings are seen here.
Therefore existence until the dissolution of beings is called samsara. As all beings are born here in the rainy seasons,
so, by rule, creatures beginning with the unmoving ones are born in kalpa after kalpa. As the marks of the seasons appear in various forms in their turn,
so the same beings are seen again in the days and nights of Brahma. At withdrawal and at emission, the moving and the fixed,
creatures go out from and enter into Prajapati in due time — Brahma, all beings, the great yogin, the great Lord.
He is the creator of all beings again and again at the beginnings of the kalpas; manifest and unmanifest is Mahadeva, and this whole world is his.
As waters, once created, flow first along a certain course on this earth and thereafter keep flowing by that same course, so do beings go to heaven.
Turning again and again in the same places through good and evil deeds, mortals, shaped by their former bodies, move upward and downward under the sun's sway.
The gods, Manus, lords of creatures, and other perfected beings who have gone to heaven, shaped by that and governed by fame and dharma, come into being again at the next creation.
Next I shall tell of time up to the dissolution of beings. The Manu periods, O twice-born, have been described by me,
fourteen of them, with the creation of creatures and with the gods; all those intervals together amount to a thousand ages.
Two full thousands of these make what is specially called a kalpa. This should be known as a day of Brahma; hear its reckoning.
A measure equal to a twinkling is made by an instant; fifteen blinks of the human eye are remembered as a kashtha.
Nine kshanas and five, twenty kashthas make three of those; a prastha with seven measures of water and a little more is remembered as a lava.
Thirty lavas should be known as a kala, and thirty kalas make a muhurta; thirty muhurtas make a day and night — such is the rule.
A day and night has somewhat more than six hundred kalas; these numbers should be understood according to the motion of the moon and sun.
Fifteen blinks make a kashtha; thirty kashthas a kala; thirty kalas a muhurta; a kala is remembered as a tenth part.
Forty-five kalas are termed a muhurta; muhurtas and lavas have been determined by those who know measures.
Likewise by this, thirteen palas of water; a prastha of water is fixed by the Magadha measure.
Four such prasthas of water make a nalika, with a hole made by four gold mashas of four finger-breadths' length.
In day and night alike, a muhurta is two nalikas; this is constant in all of these by the particular motion of the sun.
What is reckoned as more than six hundred kalas should be known as the human day; the sidereal day is ten more.
By the civil measure this human year is remembered; this is a divine day and night — such is the conclusion of the scriptures.
The reckoning by days of months, seasons, half-years and years — this knowledge is thus fixed and indicated by its terms.
The measure of kalas is called kala. What is declared as a day of Brahma is remembered as a divine crore.
Hundreds and thousands multiplied by ten and doubled, and ninety thousand, and the others as well.
Hearing this, the sages, filled with supreme wonder, then earnestly asked about the knowledge of reckoning numbers.
The sages said: We wish to hear the measure of the period of dissolution in human reckoning, in brief, in plain words.
Hearing them, the lord Vayu, devoted to the welfare of the world, spoke briefly by virtue of his divine vision.
These nights and days in the world of men were described earlier. Now I shall tell their number, the total of years at the end of Brahma's day.
Four hundred crores of human years, and thirty-two crores, have been counted by the twice-born;
and likewise eighty-nine hundred thousand and eighty thousand more — this is the period of the flood.
This is the period until the dissolution of beings, reckoned in human terms. When those worlds are burned by the seven suns, all four kinds of creatures dissolve into the great elements.
When the world is flooded with water and all moving and unmoving things have perished,
when the withdrawal is complete and Prajapati is at rest, when all is lightless, burned and covered by the darkness of night,
governed by the Lord, the single ocean then remains; it should be known as the single ocean for as long as the Lord's day lasted.
The night is the state of water; at its cessation it is remembered as day. Thus his day and night revolve in turn.
This dissolution of beings is remembered as the day and night of the Lord. All the beings in the three worlds, moving and fixed,
dissolve into the elements; hence it is called the dissolution of beings. The creatures past, present and future
are counted in divine reckoning, multiplied by the Apararddha. A Parardha doubled is declared to be the supreme lifespan.
Such is the duration here of the unborn Prajapati; at the end of his duration comes the re-dissolution of Brahma, the supreme one.
As the flame of a lamp is extinguished by a gust of wind, so Brahma is extinguished by the re-dissolution.
Likewise, when the great Lord has reabsorbed everything beginning with Mahat, Mahat dissolves into the unmanifest, and then there is equilibrium of the qualities.
Thus I have told you of the dissolution of beings. This is Brahma's occasional dissolution, the cleansing and withdrawal. It has been told in brief; what more shall I describe?
Whoever always keeps this in mind or hears it repeatedly, recites it or describes it, attains great perfection.
Suta said: Hear from me the reckoning of the Parardha and of the Para.
In counting there is one, ten, a hundred and a thousand; up to a thousand is to be known; ten thousand is an ayuta.
A hundred thousand is called a niyuta by the wise; likewise ten hundred thousand is called a prayuta.
Likewise ten thousand ayutas is called a koti; ten kotis is an arbuda, and a hundred kotis is known as an abja.
A thousand kotis the wise call a kharva; ten thousand kotis they know as a nikharva.
A hundred thousand kotis is termed a shanku; a thousand thousand kotis is called a padma.
Thousands of thousands of kotis, multiplied again by ten, those who know numbers call a samudra.
A niyuta of thousands of kotis is termed antya; a prayuta of thousands of kotis is designated madhya.
A thousand crores of crores is called a Parardha; the Parardha doubled the wise call Para.
A hundred they call parivridha, a thousand paripadmaka; after that are known ayuta, niyuta and prayuta,
arbuda, nyarbuda and kharbuda, then kharva, nikharva, shanku and padma,
samudra, antya, madhya, parardha and then para. Thus there are these eighteen places in the method of counting.
One should know those beginning with a hundred as named by the great sages. In the reckoning of kalpas, the Parardha is remembered as Brahma's.
An equal period remains for him, and at its end he comes to rest. Thus the Para and the Parardha have been counted by me in number.
Because his valour is supreme, his lifespan supreme, his austerity supreme, his power supreme, his dharma supreme, his knowledge supreme, his steadfastness supreme,
supreme Brahman, supreme wisdom and supreme lordship — therefore there is no being higher than Brahma.
Established in the supreme, he is supreme in all matters, beyond all else. Brahma is reckoned as Para, and half of it is the Parardha.
The countable and the uncountable are always technical terms; the countable is what is seen by number and is expressed up to the Apararddha.
When a heap is seen and there is no number, that is the mark of the uncountable; the endlessness seen in grains of sand is otherwise indefinable.
That reckoning is made by the lords with divine vision owing to their purity; thus, being established in knowledge, one sees everything as Brahman.
Hearing this, all those ascetics of the Naimisha forest, their eyes brimming with tears and their voices choked with joy,
all those expounders of Brahman asked Matarishvan: "O Lord, how far away is the world of Brahma, O master?
It is reckoned by yojanas; we wish to hear truly how a yojana is measured and the measure of a krosha."
Hearing their words, Matarishvan humbly spoke sweet words, as he had seen it, in due order.
Vayu said: I shall tell you this; hear what I have to say. From the unmanifest, the manifest portion, the Mahat, is described as gross.
The Bhutadi is said to be ten parts of the Mahat and gross; the measure of the Bhutadi exceeds it by ten parts.
The atom is very subtle, grasped by the mind and not by the eye; what is most indivisible in the world should be known as like an atom.
The subtle mote seen in sunlight coming through a lattice — that is declared the atom, the first of measures.
When eight atoms come together, it is called a trasarenu; that is also called lotus-dust.
Eight trasarenus are remembered as a ratharenu; eight of those together the wise call the tip of a hair.
Eight hair-tips make a liksha, eight likshas a louse, eight lice are called a barley-grain, and eight barley-grains a finger-breadth.
Twelve finger-breadths make a vitasti; a ratni should be known as twenty-one finger-breadths.
Twenty-four finger-breadths make a hasta; a kishku, two ratnis, should be known as forty-two finger-breadths.
Ninety-six finger-breadths the wise call a dhanus; this dhanus is remembered as the unit in reckoning a gavyuti.
A nali is equal to two dhanu-dandas with the same finger-breadths; three hundred dhanus is called a nalva by those who know numbers.
Two thousand dhanus are taught as a gavyuti; eight thousand dhanus make a yojana.
By this dhanus the yojana is completed. A thousand of these should be known as the distance of Shakra's krosha.
This is the reckoning of yojanas by those skilled in counting. By this measure of yojanas, hear the distance to Brahma's world.
The sun is a hundred thousand yojanas above the surface of the earth; the moon is a hundred thousand above the sun.
A full hundred thousand yojanas above the moon, the entire circle of the asterisms shines.
That hundred thousand, doubled again, is the interval of each planet above the circle of the asterisms.
Below all the star-planets moves Mercury; above it moves Venus, and above that Mars;
above that Jupiter, and above that Saturn. A hundred thousand yojanas above Saturn
the entire circle of the Seven Sages shines. A hundred thousand above the sages is described
the one who, in a small divine starry chariot, is the son of Uttanapada, Dhruva, the pivot in the sky.
This height of the three worlds has been explained by me in yojanas. In the Manu periods, the worship of the gods that is performed in the world
by the classes and stages of life proceeds in this world; it is remembered as the cause of the sustenance of all divine orders.
The three worlds have been explained; hear now what lies beyond. Above Dhruva is the Mahar world, where the dwellers of the kalpa live,
one crore of yojanas away, as it is determined. Two crores beyond the Mahar world is the Jana world,
where the sons of Brahma, Daksha and the other perfected ones, are remembered to dwell,
where the Vairaja gods dwell, free from the burning of beings. The distance from the Tapas world to the Satya world is remembered as six times as great.
That is called Brahma's world, named Apunarmaraka, where those who worship Brahma never fall again.
One crore and fifty niyutas of yojanas beyond Brahma's world is remembered as the upper part of the cosmic egg.
Fourteen crores and fifty-six niyutas is its upward extent, remembered as the furthest limit of movement.
The summit above Dhruva has been explained in yojanas as heard. I shall now tell the arrangement of the places of beings who go downward,
where living beings of terrible deeds go through their actions: the hells Raurava, the terrible Shukara and Tala,
Taptakumbha, Mahajvala, Shabala and Vimohana, Krimi, Krimibhaksha, Lalabhaksha and Vishasana,
Adhahshiras, Puyavaha and Rudhirandha, the hell strewn with excrement and that strewn with urine,
the Vaitarani, Krishna, the Asipatravana, the very terrible Agnijvala, Sandamsha and Shvabhojana,
Tamas, Kalasutra, Loha and Abhija, Apratishtha and Avichi — such are the hells.
All these dark hells lie in Yama's domain, into which evil-doers fall here, each separately.
All of them, beginning with Raurava, are declared to be below the earth. Into Raurava falls the false witness and the one who falsely accuses,
the man who is partisan and cruel. Into Shukara sinks one who is a thief, a cow-killer, a killer of embryos, one who sets fire to a city,
a slayer of a brahmin, a drinker of liquor and a stealer of gold. Into Tala falls the slayer of a kshatriya, and one who has killed a vaishya sinks there.
One who commits the killing of a brahmin, one who violates his teacher's bed, and the royal soldier likewise go to Taptakumbha;
there is tormented the merchant, the guardian of wealth who misuses it, the seller of a chaste woman, and one who abandons a devoted dependant.
Into Mahajvala goes one who approaches his daughter or daughter-in-law; those who sell the Veda and those who defile the Veda,
who despise their teachers and strike them with arrows of words, and the man who approaches forbidden women, go to the hell Shabala.
One who breaks the bounds of propriety falls into terrible Vimoha; one who performs evil sacrifices goes to Kidaloha.
One who hates gods and brahmins, who does not honour his elders, or who spoils gems, goes to Krimibhaksha.
One who eats food alone without brahmins and friends goes to the foul-smelling hell Lalabhaksha and remains there.
The arrow-maker, the potter, the stealer of coins, the physician and one who sets fire to a garden fall into Vishasana.
One who accepts gifts from the wicked, one who sacrifices for those unfit, and one who lives by astrology go to Adhomukha.
One who sells milk, liquor, salt, lac, perfumes, juices, sesame and the like falls into terrible Puyavaha.
One who confines cocks, cats, pigs, birds, deer and goats also goes to that hell.
The keeper of goats and sheep, the buffalo-keeper, the oil-presser, the brahmin who lives by the stage, one who sacrifices for a whole village,
the house-burner, the poisoner, one who eats from vessels, the seller of Soma, the drinker of liquor, the eater of meat and the killer of animals,
the butcher of buffaloes and the like, the hunter of deer, one who breaks the sacred days, the informer, and one who kills a friend —
these fall into Rudhirandha, so the wise declare. Those who cheat one seated in a row to eat
fall into the terrible hell Vidbhuja; there is no doubt of this. The man who speaks falsely and the inauspicious reviler —
that sinner falls into the terrible hell strewn with urine. Men who rob honey-gatherers go to the Vaitarani.
The mad, those broken in mind, those devoid of purity and good conduct, the wrathful, those who cause pain and the deceitful go to Krishna.
Those who cut down forests and the shepherds are cut to pieces in Asipatravana by very cruel hunters.
Those who have fallen from their stage of life fall into Agnijvala, and are devoured there by dark and spotted crows with iron beaks.
Through neglect of sacrifices, public works and vows, one falls into the hell Sandamsha; so do vowed celibates who spill their seed in daytime sleep,
and those who are taught by their sons or commanded by their sons — they all go to the hell Shvabhojana.
Those who act against the order of classes and stages of life, filled with anger and exultation — all such dwell in hell.
Above lies the great, terrible, hot Raurava; below it is remembered the very cruel, cold Tapas.
Hear them described in this order: seven hells are declared to lie below the earth,
the offspring of adharma, beginning with Andhatamisra. Raurava is the first of them, and Maharaurava;
below this again is another, remembered as the cold Tapas; the third is Kalasutra, remembered as the great serpent of many kinds;
the fourth is Apratishtha, the fifth is remembered as Avichi, the sixth is Loha, and the seventh is Avidheya.
Raurava is so called because it is terrible; it is hot and burning. The very cruel cold one below it is the lowly Tapas.
Kalasutra is declared extremely cruel, cutting everything; in Apratishtha there is no standing, and there is ever whirling.
Avichi is declared cruel because of crushing by machines; hence Loha is very cruel, because of the resort of actions there.
Because of the nature of the bodies there it is remembered as Avidheya; it is marked by pain, bondage and killing without remedy.

They are joined above and below and are remembered as lightless; in all of them the intensity of suffering is caused by adharma. Those two lightless ones meet the upper worlds; and the hell-beings there have bodies the size of towers,
born at once through their actions, able to experience the fruits; fierce, extreme suffering is remembered in all of them.
Born at once through their actions, able to experience the fruits; fierce, extreme suffering is remembered in all of them.
The torments of the hell-beings are likewise remembered as countless. There suffering is experienced, and when the karma is exhausted, again
at last they are born in animal wombs through the remainder of their karma. The gods and stars are situated above and below.
Through dharma and adharma, bodies are born at once; birth for the sake of experience comes from karma that brings about such births.
The gods see the hell-beings as facing downward and going down; and the hell-beings see all the gods as facing downward too.
Because the two are equal and their supports are by nature alike, there is no above and below in the Lokaloka.
This natural designation prevails in the Lokaloka. Then the brahmins performing the sacrificial session again spoke to Vayu.
The sages said: Of all beings dwelling in the Lokaloka, as many living creatures as wander here in samsara —
count them and tell us of them completely. Hearing the sages' words, the Wind spoke.
Vayu said: It cannot be known by divine vision or by knowledge, nor can it be counted by the eye, nor is there an end to them, O twice-born.
Because they cannot be conceived and are immeasurable, the question cannot be answered. But hear what has been designated by Brahma in number.
Whatever is the thousandth part of the unmoving beings here, that many are the earthly worms, which arise from moisture and the like.
All aquatic creatures are measured by a thousandth part of those born of moisture; let this be firmly held.
By a thousandth part of the beings that dwell in water, the birds of the world should all be known.
The thousandth part of the birds — equal to that should be known the four-footed beasts of the world.
The two-footed are measured by a thousandth of all the quadrupeds; and the righteous are measured by a thousandth of those.
By a thousandth part of the righteous are those who have gone to heaven. Whatever is the thousandth part of the righteous in heaven,
by that part are the liberated ones measured, just so many. Those dwelling in the places of torment are equal to those who attain heaven.
The fallen, the wicked who die through hatred of dharma, attain cold and heat in Raurava and in darkness.
